pieces.text: Our understanding of the atom has grown over a long time. As early as 400 BCE, a Greek philosopher named Democritus proposed that matter is composed of tiny, solid particles that are indivisible and indestructible. He called these particles
, or atoms. Democritus believed that atoms in different substances had different sizes and shapes, and these differences explained the variation in substances' properties.

textContent.text: After Democritus's early theorizing, it took more than two thousand years for a model of the atom based on experimental evidence to be developed. Between 1803 and 1807, English chemist and physicist John Dalton made experimental observations that led him to develop a new atomic theory. Dalton's model described atoms as solid, indivisible spheres.

Our understanding of the atom has grown over a long time. As early as 400 BCE, a Greek philosopher named Democritus proposed that matter is composed of tiny, solid particles that are indivisible and indestructible. He called these particles
, or atoms. Democritus believed that atoms in different substances had different sizes and shapes, and these differences explained the variation in substances' properties.

textContent.text: After Democritus's early theorizing, it took more than two thousand years for a model of the atom based on experimental evidence to be developed. Between 1803 and 1807, English chemist and physicist John Dalton made experimental observations that led him to develop a new atomic theory. Dalton's model described atoms as solid, indivisible spheres.
